newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria central bank opposes currency board plan.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria central bank opposes currency board plan.

text.p: The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) said on Wednesday that adopting a currency board as proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) would be risky.
"The introduction of a currency board at this moment would be a risky experiment," said the BNB in a statement.
The BNB also said that it was not empowered to rule on the board's introduction before parliament. The central bank gave no further details.
The IMF said on Wednesday that introduction of a currency board system would stabilise Bulgaria's national currency, curb inflation and boost economic growth.

Under a currency board -- a system introduced by some countries to boost credibility in their currency -- the amount of national currency in circulation must be matched exactly by hard currency reserves.

Such systems deprive the central bank of the usual tools of monetary management, such as market intervention and interest rates. Critics of the idea have said that unless Bulgaria boosts exports, restricted hard currency flow would stifle the economy.
"Undoubtedly the currency board can quickly reduce inflation in Bulgaria and the benefits will be worth the value of its introduction," said the IMF.
"The currency board would succeed only if it is supported by a sufficiently austere budget and broad social and political consunsus," said the statement released in Bulgarian.
Senior IMF officials are discussing with the government and bankers the introduction of a board as a means to stabilise the crumbling economy and restore confidence in the lev.
If Bulgaria agreed, it would take between two and three months to introduce the currency board, IMF officials said.

The IMF has twice postponed a $115 million loan so far due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises.
Personal and company deposits worth up to $600 million have been withdrawn from banks this year and a quarter of the country's banks were placed in receivership in a bid to prevent their collapse.

The central bank has sought the bankruptcy of 13 banks through the courts, which have not yet ruled on the cases. Delayed structural reforms and a stagnant economy have pressured the lev to 249 to the dollar on Wednesday compared with around 70 in January.
Converting lev income into dollars has become the most widespread form of saving.

The IMF said economic growth would be achieved only if inflation was reduced to less than 50 percent a year. Bulgaria's nine-month cumulative inflation stood at 154 percent, topping its annual inflation target of 105 percent.
Bulgaria sees a 10 percent decline of gross domestic product (GDP) this year. GDP has sunk by 6.2 percent in the first half of 1996.
In a bid to stabilise the lev, Bulgaria's central bank raised the central interest rate to a record-high 300 percent in September. It is currently 180 percent.
